question.title: Total costs of a juice bottler at different factory scales, with blank axes
question.alt_text: Table of monthly output 10 to 60 thousand litres with total costs N$85,000, N$120,000, N$135,000, N$160,000, N$225,000 and N$360,000; each output uses a factory built for that scale. answer.title: U-shaped long-run average cost curve with economies, optimum scale and diseconomies
answer.alt_text: Average cost (total cost divided by output) is N$8.50, 6.00, 4.50, 4.00, 4.50 and 6.00 a litre at 10 to 60 thousand litres. The LRAC curve falls to a minimum M at 40 thousand litres and N$4.00 (optimum scale), then rises. Economies of scale are labelled where it falls and diseconomies where it rises. From 20 to 40 thousand litres total cost rises from N$120,000 to N$160,000 while average cost falls from N$6.00 to N$4.00.

model.name: Binding maximum price in a competitive market for bread
model.status: illustrative: invented schedules generated from declared linear equations, not observed data
assumptions: Competitive market; the maximum price is below equilibrium, so it is binding.
The control does not shift demand or supply; quantities are read off the unchanged curves.
Quantity bought is limited to the smaller of quantity demanded and quantity supplied.

question.title: Market for bread before a maximum price
question.alt_text: Demand curve D and supply curve S for bread in a town, with price (N$ per loaf) vertically and quantity (loaves per day) horizontally. Text states that the government sets a maximum price of N$12 a loaf.

answer.title: Binding maximum price creates a shortage
answer.alt_text: Original equilibrium E at N$14 and 500 loaves a day. A maximum price of N$12, below equilibrium, is drawn as a horizontal line. Neither curve shifts: at N$12 quantity supplied is 400 loaves (on S) and quantity demanded is 600 loaves (on D), a shortage of 200 loaves a day. Only 400 loaves can be bought.

ITEM-6145-6.3-019-PROC.target: Binding minimum wage in the competitive model

model.name: Binding minimum wage in a competitive labour market for security guards
model.status: illustrative: invented schedules generated from declared linear equations; example rates, not Namibia's legal minimum wage
assumptions: Basic competitive labour market: many employers, none able to set the wage alone.
The minimum wage is above the equilibrium wage, so it is binding; a floor below N$25 would have no effect.
The floor does not shift labour demand or labour supply; employment equals labour demanded at the floor.
The result is specific to this model; it is not a claim that every minimum wage reduces employment.

question.title: Competitive labour market for security guards before a minimum wage
question.alt_text: Labour demand curve D and labour supply curve S for security guards, with wage (N$ per hour) vertically and quantity of labour (guards) horizontally. Text states that the government sets a minimum wage of N$30 an hour.

answer.title: Binding minimum wage creates an excess supply of labour in the competitive model
answer.alt_text: Original equilibrium E at N$25 an hour and 400 guards. A minimum wage of N$30, above equilibrium, is drawn as a horizontal line. Neither curve shifts: at N$30 firms want 300 guards (on D) and 500 people want to work (on S), an excess supply of labour of 200. In this model employment falls from 400 to 300.
